posts.note: Ironic 'how to short UnitedHealth' piece; several statements are reverse-psychology irony and are flagged sincere false.
Video post intro; a wish only.

statements.quote: for one human to have a “burn rate” just for meds of more than twice the annual household income? This is not sustainable. For me, or for any employer, plan member, adult, child, duck, dog, or adorable emoji.
statements.context: The author describes his own drug costs (Taltz, Xeljanz, a GLP-1) under Anthem coverage and claims a medication burn rate above twice the household income cannot last for patients, employers or plan members; an implicit call that the current Big Health cost model must change.
statements.note: Borderline: an unsustainability claim implies future change without a date.

statements.quote: some people, maybe even my readers , will make a metric ton of money betting against this nightmare scenario being sustainable.
statements.context: After quoting Wendell Potter on Aetna, the author says he is not hopeless because people will profit by betting against the sustainability of the Big Health (UnitedHealth, CVS, Aetna) business model.
statements.note: The article frames itself as ironic 'do not do this' investment satire, but this thesis reads as sincere.

statements.quote: I’ve written about automated compliance and how the #AI revolution and novel technology like will be a vector for a better future.
statements.context: Restatement of an earlier call: AI-driven automated compliance and novel technology will improve healthcare; the author links it to his citizen journalism on illegal billing and ADA noncompliance.
statements.note: Restatement of an earlier call; the source sentence has a missing word after 'like'.

statements.quote: this approach is not just ethical—it’s also very very dangerous and profitable if you can pull it off, as I will imperfectly illustrate.
statements.context: The approach is publicizing compliance failures of hospitals and payers (automated complaints, citizen journalism) while betting against Big Health; the author claims it is profitable if executed.
statements.confidence_phrase: if you can pull it off
statements.note: Conditional and compound (dangerous and profitable).

statements.quote: I have not done this myself. I own 4 whole UHC shares on the opposite hypothesis! Do not under any circumstances bet against United….
statements.context: Disclaimer inside the ironic 'how to short UnitedHealth' piece: the author discloses a small long position in UNH on the hypothesis that the stock keeps rising and advises against betting against United; the article's thrust is the opposite.
statements.note: Ironic reverse-psychology disclaimer; the sincere thesis of the piece is that Big Health is a sinking ship. Direction ambiguous.

statements.quote: “United is a sinking ship! “ Hope all of your friends can abandon UHC and its many tentacles! This is not possible. Do not do this. It’s the Titanic of health plans. It’s too big to fail. We will be FINE.
statements.context: In the satirical short-selling guide the author says the only way to make a short pay is to tell the world United is a sinking ship, then ironically denies it is possible and calls UHC the Titanic of health plans, too big to fail.
statements.note: Ironic inversion: 'too big to fail' and 'We will be FINE' read as sarcasm; the Titanic image implies the author expects a sinking. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: Driving down healthcare costs in a way that one can profit from is a business strategy. It’s also quixotic and impossible.
statements.context: Closing the list of ways to profit from lowering healthcare costs (value-based care companies, Health Rosetta brokers, Mark Cuban, PBM safe-harbor repeal), the author ironically labels the strategy impossible.
statements.note: Ironic; the article argues the opposite. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: This might be the only rational strategy for all of our future.
statements.context: After medical-debt statistics (23% of Americans, 30% of millennials), the author suggests betting against and driving down Big Health costs might be the only rational strategy for the future.
statements.note: Hedged and vague.

statements.quote: The $88 billion of current medical debt, assuming it compounds at current interest rates, with no addition to the principal, ends up looking like this in 30 years when millennials inherit the future: ... $488 billion in 30 yours is just the compounding interest on what we will owe based on the predatory Big Health financial models that have made UHC so profitable
statements.context: Numeric projection: US medical debt of $88 billion compounds to $488 billion in 30 years at current interest rates with no new principal; a chart sits between the two parts.
statements.confidence_phrase: assuming it compounds at current interest rates
statements.note: Arithmetic projection under a stated assumption; 'yours' is a typo for 'years' in the source.

statements.quote: I really just want them to know automated complaints are coming.
statements.context: Footnote 2 on Mount Sinai: the author filed an automated ADA/501(r) complaint and tells Mount Sinai that automated compliance complaints are coming to hospitals; he adds ironically that their tax-exempt status is not on the line and 'They should be fine.'
statements.note: Prediction that automated compliance complaints will spread; surrounding remarks about Mount Sinai's tax-exempt status are ironic.

statements.quote: This thread can create and ongoing reference for regulators, advocates, and lawmakers.
statements.context: The author launches a never-ending open comment thread on stimulant shortages and expects it to become an ongoing reference for regulators, advocates and lawmakers.
statements.note: Own-newsletter project (CONTROL candidate); 'and' is a typo for 'an' in the source.

statements.quote: that action would legally trigger an investigation into The AG

statements.quote: This emergency rule was filed April 13, 2023, becomes effective April 27, 2023, and expires February 6, 2024.

statements.horizon_text: becomes effective April 27, 2023, and expires February 6, 2024
statements.note: Quoted third party (regulatory text with dates); logged for recall.

statements.quote: His emergency order constitutes a serious danger to the health, safety, or welfare of a patient in that his rules effectively abruptly discontinue or prohibit gender affirming care.
statements.context: The author's assessment of the effect of the Missouri AG's emergency rule (effective April 27, 2023): it will effectively end or prohibit gender-affirming care in Missouri.
statements.note: Effect claim about a rule not yet in force at the post date.

statements.quote: Deep TMS: Most (58%) treatment-resistant patients get substantial improvement and will be replicated in large real-world data.
statements.context: List of OCD treatment options beyond EXRP; the author states the 58% response rate of Deep TMS in treatment-resistant OCD will be replicated in large real-world data.
statements.note: Claim about future real-world replication of trial data.

statements.quote: Most importantly: 31% of patients will get to full remission of symptoms.
statements.context: Same Deep TMS list item; the author states 31% of treatment-resistant OCD patients will reach full remission with Deep TMS.
statements.note: Generic rate statement phrased with 'will'; borderline forward-looking.

statements.quote: there is promising but early data on the potential role of psilocybin from ongoing research done at John’s Hopkins.
statements.context: Closing item of the OCD options list: psilocybin research at Johns Hopkins is promising but early.
statements.note: Hedged; borderline forward-looking (promise of a future role for psilocybin in OCD).

statements.quote: If you multiply that by the number of years somebody is on drugs, about 20% of people with long-term exposure to these drugs will develop TD.

statements.note: Epidemiological rate, not an event call; borderline forward-looking.
